# Chinese start-up ModelBest raises significant funding as edge AI competition intensifies

Beijing-based ModelBest secures a major C\+ Series funding round, highlighting the growing investor confidence in on-device AI amidst rising competition from tech giants like Tencent and Apple\.Beijing-based ModelBest has\.\.\.

Beijing-based ModelBest secures a major C\+ Series funding round, highlighting the growing investor confidence in on-device AI amidst rising competition from tech giants like Tencent and Apple\.

Beijing-based ModelBest has completed a C\+ Series funding round, taking its total fundraising this year to 5 billion yuan, or about $740m, as investors continue to back start-ups building AI that can run directly on devices\. Shanghai Mejoy Capital, one of the investors, said the round valued the company at 20 billion yuan, although it did not disclose how much was raised in the latest tranche\. According to the figures shared by investors, the deal underlines rising confidence in on-device AI, which promises lower latency, less dependence on remote servers and better privacy\.

Noah Intelligence has been tracking this shift as a live signal of enterprise adoption, infrastructure choices and buyer demand, where on-device AI is increasingly tied to cost, privacy and deployment constraints\.

The broader shift is being driven by the limits of cloud-based AI, where more demanding tasks still need distant data centres\. That adds cost and delay, while also creating privacy concerns when user data has to leave the handset or laptop\. As a result, developers are increasingly pursuing local, or edge, AI models that can handle more work on the device itself, even as they continue to build larger frontier systems\.

ModelBest has positioned itself as one of China’s most visible players in this area\. In May, it said its MiniCPM5-1B model, with 1 billion parameters, had been trained entirely on Huawei’s Ascend chips, reflecting a wider domestic push to make better use of locally produced AI hardware\. Independent model listings and coverage of the release say the model is designed for constrained devices, with some versions packaged for laptops and edge systems, and that it is intended to work without cloud dependence\.

The company is not alone in targeting this market\. Tencent-backed StepFun recently unveiled Step Edge, a family of on-device models aimed at low latency and offline operation, and followed that with a smartphone concept built around autonomous AI agents\. Apple is also pursuing a mixed strategy, combining external partners for high-end tasks with its own on-device models, while testing technology that claims to run much larger language models locally on an iPhone\. The competition suggests that edge AI is moving from a niche technical ambition to a central battleground in consumer technology\.

# Moonshot AI raises $3\.5B in latest funding round, eyes $30B valuation

China’s AI sector just got another reminder of how much money is chasing the next big thing\. Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based startup behind the Kimi chatbot series, has raised approximately $3\.5B in its most recent financing round, cementing its place among the best-funded AI companies to emerge from China in recent years\.

The company’s largest single raise was a roughly $2B Series D completed in May 2026, led by Meituan’s venture capital arm\. That round valued Moonshot at $20B post-money, a number that would have seemed absurd not long ago for a company founded in 2023\.

## From $300M to $20B in three years

Moonshot launched with an initial valuation of around $300M\. By February 2024, that figure had already climbed to $2\.5B\. By May 2026, it hit $20B\.

The investor roster includes Alibaba and Tencent, alongside HongShan, IDG Capital, and Gaorong Capital\.

Moonshot is now reportedly in talks targeting a valuation of over $30B in future fundraising rounds\.

## What Kimi actually does

The company’s flagship product is the Kimi chatbot, most recently updated with the Kimi K3 model released on July 16, 2026\. The headline technical feature is a context window of up to one million tokens\.

Context windows matter because they determine how much information a model can hold in memory during a single conversation or task\. One million tokens is a lot\. For reference, the average novel runs roughly 100,000 words, or somewhere in the neighborhood of 130,000 tokens\. Kimi K3 can theoretically process the equivalent of several books worth of text in a single session\.

Yang Zhilin, who founded Moonshot in 2023, previously worked at Meta AI and Google Brain\.

## What this means for the broader AI market

Moonshot is also reportedly preparing for a potential IPO in Hong Kong\. A successful public listing would do more than generate liquidity for early investors\. It would establish a public market benchmark for AI company valuations in Asia, potentially influencing how analysts and fund managers think about pricing comparable private companies across the region\.

# Accel raises $3\.5 billion to invest in emerging global AI startups

The firms new India fund is $100 million less than its predecessor, but its Europe and US funds have both grown from $650 million to $800 million\.

Accel, a global venture capital firm with offices in Silicon Valley, London and Bangalore, India, has raised $3\.5 billion in new funds for early-stage investments across the world\.

The firm, which has backed artificial intelligence companies including Anthropic, Cursor and Perplexity, has raised four separate funds dedicated to backing young startups in a moment when the AI race is upending the fundraising market\. A $1\.35 billion global expansion fund will be set aside for larger early-stage rounds and rapid follow-on investments; $800 million will target US investments, primarily in Silicon Valley; $800 million will be deployed in Europe and Israel; and $550 million in new funds will be invested in India\.

Advt

“Companies raise more money, more quickly, earlier in their company life than ever before,” said Accel partner Harry Nelis, who is based in London\. “The exciting bit is that there’s massive opportunities, but the scary bit, or the flip side, is we work with larger amounts and the risk is still pretty much the same\.”

Nelis said Accel has kept its early-stage fund sizes relatively modest when compared with many other firms, but its global expansion fund will help it invest in some of the larger rounds by splitting the investment between a core fund and the later-stage vehicle\. The firm’s new India fund is $100 million less than its predecessor, but its Europe and US funds have both grown from $650 million to $800 million\.

Over the past two years, Accel has expanded its investments from AI-native startups across the application and infrastructure layer, into more deep tech sectors, from material science to manufacturing, according to Steve Loughlin, a firm partner who is based in the San Francisco Bay Area\.

Other VC firms have also been embracing the same kinds of investments, led by a conviction that AI can help renovate complex industries in ways that traditional software did not\.

Last year, Accel joined a $300 million seed round in an AI scientific discovery platform called Periodic Labs that valued the company at $1\.3 billion\. Periodic Labs is one of a handful of startups that have raised capital under the “neolab” umbrella, a type of nascent startup that accepts massive amounts of capital at inception to fund ambitious research projects\.

Advt

Other AI startups that have raised large seed rounds include Thinking Machines Lab, which was founded by former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati and is an Accel portfolio company, and Safe Superintelligence Inc\., which was started by former OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever\.

“You can’t really construct a fund of just those types of deals,” said Loughlin, of billion-dollar seed-stage startups\. The investor said that the vast majority of Accel’s early-stage investments are in startups where it can get a meaningful ownership stake in exchange for its check\.

Part of Accel’s pitch to AI entrepreneurs is its global footprint and how it can be used to help companies expand — whether it’s boosting a US startup’s engineering resources in India, or wooing a founder based in Israel within hours because of a partner’s proximity to the region\. The firm is also attempting to build connections with the best Silicon Valley talent by launching a no-strings-attached, in-person residency program for aspiring founders that’s located next door to its San Francisco office\.The fundraising haul comes at a time of change for the firm, which was founded in 1983\.

Advt

One of its most prominent early-stage investors, Daniel Levine, who backed Scale AI and Vercel, will no longer make investments for Accel in this fund or future funds, an Accel spokesperson confirmed\. Despite stepping back from his role, Levine remains a partner and will continue to serve on his board seats and support his existing investments\.

Additionally, the firm has accelerated its pace for its later-stage investments, recently raising $5 billion in capital for that purpose, as Bloomberg News previously reported\.

# Singapore start-up Ropedia raises US$22 mil in pre-Series A round for robot-training data

The robotics data company has raised US$30 million so far, and will use the latest funds to gather more training data, increase device production and expand in Singapore and the US\.

Ropedia, a Singapore start-up that supplies training data for robots and physical artificial intelligence systems, has raised US$22 million \($28\.4 million\) in a pre-Series A funding round\.

It did not identify the investors in the latest round, saying only that it was led by venture firms with experience in AI, deep technology and infrastructure in Southeast Asia\.

The deal brings its total funding to US$30 million\. An earlier round included investors and individuals connected to Google, Andreessen Horowitz, Nvidia and Amazon, according to the company\.

Ropedia's proprietary wearable devices record first-person video, depth, movement and audio as people carry out physical tasks\. The company processes that information into training material for developers seeking to teach robots how to perform tasks in real-world settings\. It offers the data through its Xperience-10M product and customised services\.

\"A robot can't play baseball by watching a video any more than you could learn to ride a bike by reading about it\. The robot must understand what it's like to grip a bat and know the timing it takes to hit a ball\. That's the information Ropedia's technology provides, and it's why this investment matters,\" says Zhaoxi Chen, CEO and co-founder of Ropedia\.

He continues: \"Our technology lets robots capture the experience and real judgment it will take for them to move through the world\. If we get all that right, the robots will leave the beta stage and start doing real work, first in factories, then at home, with families\.\"

According to Ropedia, its approach can reduce data-collection costs by as much as 50 times compared with traditional methods\.

Its wearable device has entered mass production, and the company is already working with more than 20 robotics and foundation-model companies in North America, China and Singapore\.

Ropedia will use the fresh funds to expand data collection in Southeast Asia and North America, increase production of its wearable devices and grow its teams in Singapore and the US\.

It also plans to add tools for annotating and checking data, strengthen its compliance systems and expand research into data foundation models and world models\.

Ropedia was founded in the second half of 2025 by Chen, chief technology officer Fangzhou Hong and chief scientist Ziwei Liu, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University\.

# Whatnot funding round lifts founders’ wealth as live shopping gains traction in U\.S\.

Live shopping platforms are drawing fresh investor attention as real-time auctions expand across the U\.S\. Whatnot’s latest capital raise values the Los Angeles company at $20 billion and pushes its two co-founders into multibillionaire territory\.

## Highlights

- Whatnot's $545 million funding round boosts its valuation to $20 billion, significantly increasing founders Grant LaFontaine and Logan Head's paper wealth\.
- Bloomberg Billionaires Index reports LaFontaine and Head are now each worth over $2\.8 billion following the latest capital raise\.
- The funding and valuation jump highlight growing momentum for live commerce in the U\.S\. and signal strong investor confidence in interactive mobile auction platforms\.

## Funding round and valuation jump

As reported by Bloomberg, citing Bloomberg Billionaires Index, Whatnot’s latest funding round increases the paper wealth of Chief Executive Officer Grant LaFontaine and Chief Technology Officer Logan Head to more than $2\.8 billion each\. The index is valuing their fortunes for the first time after the company announced on Friday that it raised $545 million\.

The Los Angeles-based e-commerce company says the round values Whatnot at $20 billion\. The funding comes after last week’s raise and reflects investor backing for the app’s fast-paced live auction model\.

## Momentum for live commerce in U\.S\.

Whatnot’s valuation increase underscores the growing appeal of live shopping formats in the U\.S\., where consumers are increasingly using mobile platforms to buy through interactive auctions\. The company’s latest raise also signals that investors see further expansion potential in the segment\.

The gains for LaFontaine and Head place both founders among newly minted multibillionaires as the sector attracts more attention from capital markets\. Their holdings rise alongside Whatnot’s higher valuation, linking founder wealth directly to the company’s latest financing milestone\.

In our earlier article on Intel’s plan to issue at least $15 billion in new stock, we explained how AI-driven demand for server and data-center chips has lifted valuations and encouraged the company to raise fresh capital\. We also noted that much of the funding is expected to support Intel’s foundry expansion, even as the company’s valuation implies ambitious growth assumptions and leaves limited room for execution missteps\.

# Robotics startup Generalist AI is in talks to raise a new funding round at a $3 billion valuation

Venture firm 8VC is expected to lead the round, according to people familiar with the discussions\.

The round is in progress, and details could change\. Generalist AI and 8VC did not respond to requests for comment\.

It's the latest example of investors pouring money into physical AI AI systems that can act in the real world\. Generalist is competing with startups like Physical Intelligence, valued at more than $11 billion, Skild AI, valued at more than $14 billion, Field AI, valued at $2 billion, and Genesis AI, which is in talks to raise funding at a $3 billion valuation\.

The fresh funding comes just one month after Generalist announced it had raised $400 million to develop more sophisticated AI models for robots\. That round valued the company at $2 billion and was led by Radical Ventures, with participation from 8VC, Union Square Ventures, Nvidia, and Bezos Expeditions\.

Generalist was founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind robotics researchers Pete Florence and Andy Zeng and former Boston Dynamics roboticist Andrew Barry\.

Generalists' angel investors include Xiaomi cofounder Bin Lin, Stanford professor and World Labs cofounder Fei-Fei Li, and AngelList cofounder Naval Ravikant\.

Generalist is building the AI brains that power robots\. Its models are designed to work across different robots and environments, from factories and laboratories to homes and space\. Rather than building robots itself, the startup is developing the intelligence that allows machines to understand and act in the physical world\.

Its latest model, GEN-1, is designed to teach robots basic physical tasks\. Generalist has released videos showing robots powered by its software performing dexterous tasks, including folding laundry, sorting Lego bricks, and using a whisk to mix baking ingredients\.

# China’s Moonshot AI in talks on pre-IPO funds at US$50 billion value

This should mark the final infusion of capital for Moonshot before an IPO as soon as 2026

Published Wed, Jul 22, 2026 · 10:18 AM

MOONSHOT AI is preparing to begin discussions in August on a final round of fundraising before listing in Hong Kong, capitalising on the excitement around its latest model to raise capital at a valuation of as much as US$50 billion\.

The Chinese AI lab should close in coming days a financing round that began in summer 2026 at a valuation of US$31\.5 billion, people familiar with the matter said\. Once finalised, Moonshot then intends to immediately open discussions with potential backers about a follow-on capital-raising, the people said, asking to remain unidentified to talk about a private deal\. That should mark the final infusion of capital for Moonshot before an initial public offering as soon as 2026\.

The speed with which Moonshot is tapping capital markets underscores investor interest in a startup that has upended perceptions of how far Chinese artificial intelligence technology lags American\. The 2\.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 – billed as the world’s largest open-weight AI model – surprised developers and investors with performance approaching the latest frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic\. Representatives for the company did not respond to an e-mailed request for comment\.

Moonshot now seeks to ride that momentum\. It aims to complete the dismantling of its offshore red-chip structure by the end of July, paving the way for the domestic fundraising and its broader IPO preparations, the people said\.

Chinese firms typically raise money at a velocity near-unparalleled in the US, particularly during periods when they are dominating headlines or when their sector is hot\. In Moonshot’s case, the speed with which it is moving also stems from its business prospects\.

Moonshot achieved US$300 million of annual recurring revenue – a gauge of future sales – in June, jumping from US$200 million in April, Bloomberg News reported earlier\. Since the K3’s launch, daily sales have surged at least six times, one person familiar with the matter has said\.

The explosive debut of its latest AI model on Jul 17 was a vindication of sorts for founder Yang Zhilin, the reclusive 33-year-old alumnus of Carnegie Mellon University, Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google\.

Yang founded the 300-person outfit along with several technologists from China’s prestigious Tsinghua University, including the lead guitarist of a band he started\. They named the company’s Chinese corporate entry after Dark Side of the Moon, Yang’s favourite Pink Floyd album\.

Kimi K3 outperformed all rivals except for Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5\.6 on overall capability, according to Artificial Analysis\.

SEE ALSO

More

Elon Musk lauded the model as “impressive,” while OpenAI’s head of strategy, Dean Ball, warned that the open-weight release pushes the tech world closer to “full AI communism\.”

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday \(Jul 21\) that the US will carefully examine open source AI models created overseas, including those from China, and take action on any evidence of intellectual property theft from US companies\.

Moonshot’s existing investors include Chinese tech leaders Meituan and Tencent Holdings; renowned venture capital firms IDG Capital, HSG and ZhenFund; and state-backed players China Mobile and the Beijing AI Industry Investment Fund\. BLOOMBERG
